extracted.intended_audience: novelists and students of the craft of fiction; writers studying narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical guidance about methods for composing novels: how to use scene vs. pictorial description, point of view, preparation, time, and climax. Emphasises matching method to subject and building descriptive groundwork that supplies dramatic force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of narrative voice and its effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of the first person (placing a story 'in the mouth of a man who was there on the spot') alters how a story functions — it can be 'the first step towards the dramatization of a story' or can pass the drama 'through a man's thought and catch his reflection of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose point of view according to subject: first-person narration can enhance plain narrative by dramatizing events (as in Esmond) or by toning/qualifying action (as in The Master of Ballantrae). Consider what the subject needs — enhancement of drama, pictorial impression, or inner reflection — before committing to first person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary pictorial description as preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'pictured scene that opens and spreads very gradually' provides a valid world for a drama that could not be precipitated forthwith; Balzac's method is to offer clear, business-like descriptions of place as an essential preliminary to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay down a detailed, precise scene (streets, houses, rooms, furniture, objects) early so that later events inherit continuity and reality; such preparation 'secures the sense of time' and supplies a reserve of force for the climax. Ensure the picture exists in your imagination rather than as a mechanical inventory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of setting to embody character and history
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac 'cannot think of his people without the homes they inhabit' — the house or inanimate setting 'incarnates all the past of its old owner' and visibly links it to the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ environment, architecture, furnishings and routine as expressive elements that reveal character, social condition, and past. The setting should function as presence and influence throughout the story, not merely backdrop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Securing the sense of time through picture rather than prolonged interior narration
rubrics_metrics.description: By preparing the scene thoroughly, Balzac can say casually, 'Five years went by in this way,' and still have the reader feel the slow crawling of time because 'his preliminary picture included the representation of time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a story's principal fact is duration, build a composite, enduring impression early so you can summarize later without losing the felt passage of years. Avoid attempting to show long stretches only through extended interior monologue if the scene can supply the temporal sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of preparation and concealment of artifice
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax 'ought to be free to do what it must without any unnecessary distraction' and the art of preparation 'is no art if it betrays itself at the outset.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve effects and avoid obvious signaling; prepare and anticipate in earlier pages but keep the devices unobtrusive so that the reader perceives the effect when it is used, not the fact of preparation itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match method to subject (external picture vs. internal study)
rubrics_metrics.description: For subjects that lack inner resonance (e.g., Eugenie), closer participation in her romance 'would infallibly be lowered' — it is 'much better to look at it from outside' and note incidents rather than cast the book as interior consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the material supports intense interior exploration; if the subject is 'scanty' or has little incident, prefer external, pictorial treatment that provides dramatic and temporal substance rather than forcing psychological deep-dives that may wear thin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build sufficient descriptive substance to allow repetition and progressive devastation
rubrics_metrics.description: In La Recherche de l'Absolu Balzac 'amasses in his opening picture the reserve of effect that he needs' so that the repeated blows of ruin are 'renewed and increased by the sight of the spreading devastation around him.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a story depends on repeated similar effects (e.g., recurring disappointments), create a rich, tangible world at the outset so that each repetition accrues force by showing gradual destruction or change in that world rather than by recycling the same incident alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and limits of method (dramatic/episodic vs pictorial/expository)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolstoy's plan in Anna Karenina is 'strictly dramatic' — a chain of particular occasions — whereas Balzac uses freedom of exposition and retrospect; trusting a single method 'too far' can cause miscalculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a coherent plan (scenic, episodic drama vs. broad pictorial exposition) and be aware of each method's limits. Mixing is possible but should be handled with care; do not expect one method to fulfill tasks it is unsuited for without supplementary devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designing the climax to complete the work organically
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax 'ought to complete, to add the touch that makes the book whole and organic' and should be 'free to do what it must' with nothing left for it to accomplish but the necessary touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve only what the climax must deliver; avoid burdening the climax with unresolved preparatory tasks. Use prior preparation to despatch subsidiary matters so the climax can fulfill its unique, unencumbered purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and quickness of characterization by small details
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolstoy 'can create a character in so few words' — he 'catches the passing thought' and makes even minor figures 'centres of vision' by brief, telling details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reveal personality through small, well-chosen gestures, passing thoughts, and scene actions rather than long expository biographies. This economy lets many characters be rendered naturally within episodic or crowded narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority of knowledge in descriptive detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac's cataloguing succeeds because 'the place exists in his thought' — he reproduces it 'inch by inch, fact by fact' without losing the whole; by contrast, an impressionist would produce a mechanical sum of details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid listing details mechanically; only exhaustive, precise description that comes from genuine imaginative possession of a scene will read alive. Make sure every concrete fact you offer is grounded in an imagined, coherent space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid needless expatiation on monotony or interior states
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is little incident (Eugenie's long waiting), Balzac refrains from 'dwelling upon the shades of her long disappointment' because her endurance and fidelity are 'fully created in the book before they are put to the test.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a character's inner life risks being thinly sustained, rely on indirect methods (scene, setting, prior implication) instead of prolonged interior narration. Let the book's earlier images carry the weight of later emotional developments.
